holidays.name: National Chinese Almond Cookie Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the crumbly, buttery, almond-flavored cookie that shows up at Chinese restaurants and bakeries. Pour some tea, grab a cookie, and let the crumbs fall where they may.
holidays.origin: Like many American food days, it appeared through food-industry and online calendar listings rather than an official proclamation. The cookie itself is tied to Cantonese-style bakeries and was popularized in Chinese American restaurants.
holidays.funFact: Chinese almond cookies traditionally have a single almond or an almond-shaped press on top, and in many Chinese communities they are associated with good luck and celebrations.

holidays.name: National Name Yourself Day
holidays.description: A day dedicated to the delightfully absurd idea of picking a new name for yourself, whether a nickname, a stage name, or a fantasy alter ego. Time to finally become Captain Waffles or Duchess Thunderpants.
holidays.origin: It is an unofficial, whimsical observance that circulates in lists of offbeat holidays. It encourages people to playfully reinvent themselves, if only for the day.
holidays.funFact: Many famous people did choose their own names. Stage names like Elton John (born Reginald Dwight) and Lady Gaga (born Stefani Germanotta) became more famous than the originals.

holidays.name: Unicorn Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the mythical, sparkly, rainbow-maned unicorn. Expect glitter, horn headbands, and a suspicious number of pastel-colored foods.
holidays.origin: Unicorn Day is an unofficial, internet-era celebration that grew along with the unicorn trend in fashion, food, and toys. It gives fans of the mythical creature an excuse to go full sparkle.
holidays.funFact: The unicorn is Scotland's national animal. It has been featured on the Royal Coat of Arms of Scotland for centuries.

holidays.name: National Gin and Tonic Day
holidays.description: A toast to the crisp, fizzy cocktail of gin, tonic water, and a wedge of lime. It is a refreshing drink with a surprisingly medical backstory.
holidays.origin: Like many drink days, it is an unofficial observance promoted by cocktail lovers and spirits brands. The drink dates back to British colonial India, where tonic water was used to deliver quinine.
holidays.funFact: Tonic water contains quinine, which was used to prevent malaria. British officers in India reportedly mixed it with gin to make it more palatable, which helped create the classic cocktail.

holidays.name: Winston Churchill Day
holidays.description: A commemoration of Winston Churchill, the British wartime Prime Minister known for his speeches, his cigars, and his legendary one-liners.
holidays.origin: On April 9, 1963, U.S. President John F. Kennedy proclaimed Churchill an honorary citizen of the United States, which made him the first person so honored by an act of Congress.
holidays.funFact: Churchill was also a prolific painter and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953, which is a pretty strong side hustle for a politician.
